title: The Early Church Era
tag: The apostles' children, under an empire that could turn on them
stepStatus: Part of Phase One (Step 0 COMPLETE) - Phase One deliberately spans Eras 1-2, creed to council
rec: Part of Phase One — the Step 0 selection record is on file.
shortDescription: From the burning of Jerusalem's Temple in 70 to Constantine's victory at Rome in 312, churches grew in cities from Lyons and Rome to Carthage, Alexandria, Asia Minor and Edessa. Through these years, emperors at times ordered Christians punished and their churches torn down.

timeline.headline: The Temple falls, and Rome sets its first rule for Christians

lines.text: The church of Jerusalem leaves the city for Pella, a town of Perea, commanded, Eusebius says, by a revelation given before the war.
Titus's army burns the Temple, and Jerusalem is taken in the second year of the emperor Vespasian.
lines.reference: Josephus, Jewish War VI.4.7 and VI.10.1 (Whiston), cic/texts/josephus_works-antiquities-wars-life_whiston1859.txt lines 126015-126020, 127565-127567

lines.text: Pliny, a governor troubled by the number of martyrs, writes to Trajan that Christians rise at dawn to sing hymns to Christ as a God. Trajan rules that Christians are not to be sought out, but are to be punished when found.
No great persecution follows, Eusebius says, but local ones go on in particular provinces, stirred up sometimes by the people and sometimes by the rulers.

timeline.headline: Churches across the empire, tested from within and attacked from without

lines.text: In the Roman province of Asia, the faithful meet often, in many places, to examine the sayings of the New Prophecy. They reject it and bar its followers from communion.
lines.reference: The anonymous writer quoted by Eusebius, Church History V.16.10, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 29721-29738

lines.text: In the seventeenth year of the emperor Antoninus Verus, crowds in the cities turn on the Christians, and the churches of Lyons and Vienne in Gaul send an account of their martyrs.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History V, Introduction 1, and V.1.1-2, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 26706-26707, 26736-26739, 26796-26804

timeline.headline: Carthage and Edessa come into view, and Decius persecutes the churches

lines.text: At Edessa, a flood breaks the city wall and destroys the temple of the church of the Christians.
lines.note: The chronicle dates it to the year 513 of its own reckoning.

lines.when: in the reigns of Severus and Caracalla
lines.text: Tertullian, from Carthage in the province of Africa, writes his many books in Latin.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 53, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40495-40499

lines.text: Decius succeeds Philip as emperor and begins a persecution of the churches. Fabianus, bishop of Rome, is put to death.
At Alexandria, Bishop Dionysius writes, the persecution began a whole year before the emperor's decree.

timeline.headline: A quarrel over baptism, a second persecution, then peace and plague

lines.text: At Carthage, Cyprian, pastor of the church there, holds that those who come over from heresy must be baptized before they are received. Stephen, bishop of Rome, holds that this adds something new against tradition.
Valerian, friendly to Christians at first, is persuaded to turn on them, Dionysius writes.

Valerian is taken captive by the barbarians. His son Gallienus stops the persecution by public proclamation, and in a letter to the bishops lets them carry out their duties freely and orders others out of their places of worship.
After war and famine, a plague follows. Dionysius writes that most of the Christians nursed the sick without fear, and many died with them.

timeline.headline: The Great Persecution, and its end

lines.text: In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, in March, near Easter, imperial edicts order the churches leveled and the Scriptures burned.
Eusebius writes that he saw with his own eyes the houses of prayer thrown down and the Scriptures burned in the marketplaces.

The emperor who began the persecution, struck by a loathsome illness, orders it stopped. A decree in the name of Galerius and his fellow emperors bids Christians rebuild their churches and pray for the emperor.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VIII.16.3-5 and VIII.17.1-3, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 45403-45434, 45443-45457

lines.text: Constantine marches on Rome and defeats Maxentius, who drowns when the bridge of boats he built over the river breaks.

uncertain: The move to Pella. Eusebius says a revelation commanded the church of Jerusalem to leave before the war, and gives no year.

How the churches of Alexandria and Edessa began. Eusebius gives Mark's founding of the churches of Alexandria as something people say. He says the apostle Thomas sent Thaddeus to Edessa, from records he says were taken from the archives of Edessa. The first dated mention of a church building at Edessa is the flood in the reign of Severus.

How steady the persecutions were. Eusebius says that after Trajan's ruling there was no great persecution for a time, only local ones in particular provinces; the hunts under Decius, Valerian and Diocletian were ordered by the emperors themselves.
The era's title and its end in 312 are the map's labels for the age, not dates the old sources give.
